articles.title_original: Many-Body Ground State Manifold of Flat Band Interacting Hamiltonian for Magic Angle Twisted Bilayer Graphene
articles.title_en: Theory Defines Ground-State Manifold in Magic-Angle Twisted Bilayer Graphene
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract At a magic relative twist angle, magic angle twisted bilayer graphene (MATBG) has an octet of flat bands that can host strong correlation physics when partially filled. A key theoretical discovery in MATBG is the existence of ferromagnetic Slater determinants as exact ground states of the corresponding flat band interacting (FBI) Hamiltonian. The FBI Hamiltonian describes the behavior of electrons that interact with each other in a high-dimensional space, and is constructed from the band structure of the non-interacting Bistritzer–MacDonald model at the chiral limit. A key property of the FBI Hamiltonian for MATBG is that it is frustration-free and can be written as a sum of non-commuting terms. In this work, we provide a complete characterization of the ground state manifold of the FBI Hamiltonian, proving that it is precisely the linear span of such ferromagnetic Slater determinants.
articles.summary_en: Researchers theoretically characterize the complete ground-state manifold of the flat-band interacting Hamiltonian for magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene. The work establishes that it is precisely spanned by ferromagnetic Slater determinants, advancing understanding of strong-correlation physics in twisted graphene systems.

articles.title_original: Improving High‐Temperature Operational Stability of Inverted Perovskite Solar Cells Through MXene Heat‐Dissipating Layers
articles.title_en: Functionalized MXene layers quadruple high-temperature stability of inverted perovskite solar cells
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Despite inverted perovskite solar cells (iPSCs) having reached power conversion efficiencies (PCEs) of about 27% with long‐term stability at room temperature, their commercial devices must prevent heat‐induced performance degradation. In PSCs, 2D MXenes have been employed to enhance their long‐term stability at high temperatures; however, a deep understanding of the heat management mechanism of applying MXenes at interfaces is still lacking. Herein, we investigate the application of MeO‐2PACz‐functionalized MXenes at the hole transport layer (HTL) interface in iPSCs using MeO‐2PACz as the HTL. PSCs reached PCEs of 23.02 ± 1.14%, observing a 400% enhancement in their operational stability, spanning the T 80 lifetime at 65°C from 141 to 687 h. HAADF‐STEM imaging and STEM‐EELS analysis confirmed the effective intercalation of the MeO‐2PACz within the MXene atomic nanolayers. Thermal conductivity measurements and simulations revealed that the application of the functionalized MXenes can effectively dissipate the heat from the perovskite absorber, reducing the perovskite temperature by about 20 ± 6%. Overall, the fourfold extension of T 80 by using MeO‐2PACz‐functionalized MXenes in iPSCs is attributed to the synergy between reduced thermal accumulation and improved buried‐interface quality, including defect passivation, enhanced charge extraction, and suppressed ion migration.
articles.summary_en: Researchers used MeO-2PACz-functionalized MXene layers at the hole-transport interface to reduce perovskite temperature by about 20 ± 6%. The approach extended the cells’ 65°C T80 lifetime from 141 to 687 hours while achieving a power-conversion efficiency of 23.02 ± 1.14%.

articles.title_original: Interlayer‐Tailored MXene@MWCNT Heterostructures Enabling Superior Charge Storage in Aqueous Electrolytes
articles.title_en: MXene–MWCNT Heterostructure Improves Aqueous Energy Storage
articles.excerpt_original: The intentional design of hybrid nanoarchitectures is crucial for achieving enhanced electrochemical performance in next‐generation energy storage systems. These designs must facilitate rapid ion transport, provide numerous active surface sites, and maintain effective electron‐transfer pathways. In this study, an MXene@MWCNT heterostructure was rationally engineered via a solvothermal strategy to integrate the redox‐active surface chemistry of MXene with the high electrical conductivity and mechanical robustness of multiwalled carbon nanotubes (MWCNT). The structural stability and compositional integrity of the heterostructure were rigorously confirmed by XRD, FESEM, EDS, FTIR, BET, and Raman spectroscopy, which collectively verified effective interfacial coupling without observable phase degradation. Raman spectroscopy revealed an optimized defect–graphitic balance, with an I D /I G ratio of 0.99 and a high I 2D /I G ratio of 0.97, indicative of abundant electrochemically active sites and well‐preserved conductive domains. Owing to the synergistic contributions of electric double‐layer capacitance and pseudocapacitive charge‐storage mechanisms, the MXene@MWCNT electrode exhibits a high specific capacitance of 232 F g −1 at 10 mV s −1 , along with excellent rate performance and cycling stability. These results underscore the effectiveness of interfacial nanoengineering in MXene‐based hybrids and highlight a viable pathway toward high‐performance, sustainable aqueous energy storage systems.
articles.summary_en: Researchers engineered an MXene@MWCNT heterostructure using a solvothermal method, combining MXene pseudocapacitance with the conductivity and mechanical robustness of multiwalled carbon nanotubes. The electrode delivered 232 F g−1 at 10 mV s−1, with strong rate performance and cycling stability.

articles.title_original: Nanoconfined Liquid-Liquid Transition Photonic Synapse: Experimental Architecture and Optical Contrast Analysis
articles.title_en: Proposed hBN Nanocavity Enables Liquid–Liquid Transition Photonic Synapse
articles.excerpt_original: Description / Abstract We propose a conceptual architecture for an artificial photonic synapse based on the liquid-liquid transition (LLT) of an ionic liquid nanoconfined within a hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) cavity. Unlike conventional phase-change memories relying on amorphous/crystalline transitions, the proposed approach exploits the structural nanosegregation of ionic liquids as a potential mechanism for analog optical modulation. The central hypothesis is that changes in the nanostructural state of the confined ionic liquid could modify its effective dielectric properties, producing a measurable variation in refractive index or optical transmission. A Fabry-Pérot cavity is proposed as an optical amplification mechanism. The work defines a three-stage experimental validation program: (1) macroscopic proof-of-concept characterization, (2) fabrication of a sealed hBN nanocavity, and (3) characterization of reproducible multi-level optical states. Six major physical challenges are identified, including persistence of the LLT under confinement, domain cooperativity, optical contrast, thermal stability, cell-to-cell variability, and lateral thermal crosstalk in hBN. No functional photonic synapse is claimed. The objective is to establish a low-cost, quantitative and falsifiable experimental pathway capable of validating or rejecting the underlying physical hypothesis.
articles.summary_en: Researchers propose an artificial photonic synapse using an ionic liquid confined in a hexagonal boron nitride nanocavity to produce analog optical modulation. The work outlines experimental validation steps but reports no functional device, with key uncertainties including confinement stability, optical contrast, and thermal crosstalk.

articles.title_original: Nitride MXenes Beyond Carbides: Bridging the Gap Between Computational Prediction and Experimental Realization
articles.title_en: Review Identifies Synthesis Barriers to Nitride MXene Realization
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Two‐dimensional transition‐metal nitride MXenes represent a promising yet largely unrealized branch of the MXene family. Compared with carbide analogues, they exhibit stronger M–N bonding, distinct surface chemistry, and lattice‐nitrogen‐mediated reaction pathways. Despite extensive computational predictions of thermodynamically viable compositions, only a limited number of nitride MXenes have been experimentally realized, revealing a persistent gap between theoretical design and laboratory synthesis. This review examines this disparity by linking nitride MAX‐phase stability, selective A‐layer removal, nitrogen retention, and phase verification. Nitride MAX phases occupy narrow thermodynamic stability windows relative to competing binary nitrides, while conventional fluoride‐based etching often fails to selectively remove the A layer without destabilizing the M–N framework. Elevated‐temperature processing further promotes nitrogen loss and competing‐phase formation. Recent advances in molten‐salt, Lewis‐acidic, electrochemical, ammoniation, and vapor‐phase synthesis routes are critically evaluated according to the mechanistic barriers they address. Particular attention is given to structural validation because layered morphology alone does not establish MXene formation. To bridge the computational‐experimental gap, we propose a multidimensional workflow integrating precursor stability, bonding descriptors, environment‐dependent etching thermodynamics, kinetic selectivity, surface termination evolution, and iterative experimental feedback. These perspectives establish synthesis and validation priorities required to transform nitride MXenes into reproducible, application‐relevant two‐dimensional nitrides.
articles.summary_en: This review examines why computationally predicted nitride MXenes remain difficult to synthesize reproducibly, highlighting instability, nitrogen loss, competing phases, and limitations of conventional etching. It evaluates alternative synthesis routes and proposes an integrated workflow for validating application-relevant materials.

articles.title_original: Evolution and breakdown of chiral anomaly in Weyl semiconductor tellurium
articles.title_en: Doped Tellurium Shows Tunable Chiral Anomaly and Room-Temperature Magnetoresistance
articles.excerpt_original: Chiral anomaly in topological materials manifests as negative longitudinal magnetoresistance, yet the tunability and evolution of this effect remain elusive. Here we show that doped tellurium serves as a versatile platform to realize a giant negative longitudinal magnetoresistance that is highly tunable via the Fermi level and magnetic field. By moving the Fermi level towards the Weyl point, we observe a pronounced enhancement of negative magnetoresistance, which arises from chiral anomaly and robustly persists up to ambient temperature. Beyond the quantum limit, the system exhibits positive linear magnetoconductance, serving as a compelling transport signature of the chiral anomaly in the lowest Landau level. Notably, in the extreme quantum limit at cryogenic temperatures, the magnetoresistance undergoes a dramatic reversal from negative to positive. This reversal points to a potential field-induced phase transition into a collective electronic state driven by enhanced electron–electron interactions. Our findings provide valuable insights into the unconventional chiral transport and emergent correlated quantum states under extreme magnetic fields. Tellurium is an elemental Weyl semiconductor that hosts unique massless Weyl fermions. By tuning its electronic properties and applying strong magnetic fields, we reveal a giant and highly controllable negative magnetoresistance that persists up to room temperature, and its dramatic reversal at high fields uncovers a new collective electronic state.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrate highly tunable negative longitudinal magnetoresistance in doped tellurium, persisting to ambient temperature through Fermi-level and magnetic-field control. At extreme fields and cryogenic temperatures, the effect reverses sign, indicating a possible field-induced collective electronic state.

articles.title_original: DFT Study of Triaxial Magnetic Anisotropy and Strain-Induced Easy-Axis Switching in Ferromagnetic CrTe3 Monolayer for Spintronic Applications
articles.title_en: Strain-Controlled Magnetic Anisotropy Demonstrated in CrTe3 Monolayer
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Magnetic anisotropy is essential for stabilizing long-range magnetic order against thermal fluctuations in two-dimensional (2D) materials. However, the precise interplay between magnetic anisotropy and electronic structure in many emerging 2D magnetic semiconductors remains poorly understood. In this work, we systematically investigate the electronic structure and magnetic properties of the CrTe3 monolayer using first-principles density functional theory calculations. Our results identify the CrTe3 monolayer as a ferromagnetic semiconductor with an indirect band gap of 0.45 eV, exhibiting a distinctive triaxial magnetic anisotropy. Further analysis demonstrates that this anisotropy originates from the combined contributions of magnetic dipole−dipole interactions (shape anisotropy) and spin−orbit coupling (magnetocrystalline anisotropy). Importantly, we show that the easy magnetization axis can be effectively manipulated and even switched by applying external strain, with the most dramatic response observed under uniaxial tensile strain along the y-direction. Monte Carlo simulations yield a Curie temperature of 134 K for the pristine monolayer, which can be further enhanced under applied strain. Our work not only elucidates the microscopic origin of triaxial magnetic anisotropy in the CrTe3 monolayer but also provides a comprehensive understanding of strain-mediated magnetic control in 2D ferromagnetic semiconductors.
articles.summary_en: DFT calculations identify monolayer CrTe3 as a ferromagnetic semiconductor with triaxial magnetic anisotropy and a 0.45 eV indirect band gap. Applied strain can switch its easy magnetization axis and raise its predicted Curie temperature, supporting potential spintronic applications.

articles.title_original: Magnetic graphene oxide improves the expression of some human cumulus cells biomarkers

articles.excerpt_original: Purpose: Developing non-invasive, accurate methods for selecting high-implantation embryos is crucial for assisted reproductive technologies (ART). Cumulus cells (CCs) are reliable indicators of oocyte quality. This study investigated the effects of magnetic graphene oxide (MGO) on the viability, apoptosis, oxidative status, and proliferation-related proteins of human CCs in vitro. Methods: Human CCs were treated with MGO (1.5–400 µg/mL) for 24, 48, and 72 hours. Viability was assessed via MTT and Annexin V-FITC/PI flow cytometry. Expression of apoptosis-related (Bcl-2, Bax, cleaved/pro-caspase-3), antioxidant (Nrf2, SOD2), and cell-cycle (cyclin D1) proteins was analyzed using Western blotting. Additionally, Catalase (CAT) activity, Reduced glutathione (GSH), and total antioxidant capacity (TAC) were determined using colorimetric assays. Results: MGO showed dose- and time-dependent effects, with low concentrations showing high biocompatibility at 48 hours. Flow cytometry revealed MGO significantly increased cell viability from 88.06±1.7% (control) to 94.58±2.88%, 92.87±0.43%, 97.09±2.69%, and 97.61±1.72% at 3.125, 12.5, 50, and 100 µg/mL, respectively (p < 0.0001), while total apoptosis decreased from 11.05±0.55% to 4.96±0.27%, 6.74±0.46%, 2.50±0.21%, and 2.16±0.10% (p < 0.0001). MGO upregulated Bcl-2 (p < 0.001), Nrf2 (>2-fold, p < 0.0001), SOD2 (>2.5-fold, p < 0.0001), and cyclin D1 (1.5-fold, p < 0.01), but downregulated Bax (p < 0.05) and cleaved caspase-3 (p < 0.0001). CAT, GSH, and TAC were significantly elevated (p < 0.001). Conclusion: Low concentrations of MGO enhanced human CC viability, reduced apoptosis, and boosted antioxidant defenses and proliferation-related pathways. These findings suggest MGO’s biomedical potential in cell survival and anti-apoptotic

articles.title_original: Printed Devices with MXene Active Layers and Their Applications
articles.title_en: Printed MXene Devices for Flexible Electronics and Energy Applications
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract MXenes have demonstrated strong potential across a wide range of applications due to their outstanding properties, evidenced by the impressive performance of MXene-based devices reported to date. As the field moves toward commercialization, identifying methods and technologies compatible with scalable manufacturing has become increasingly important. In this context, direct-write printing has emerged as a transformative approach in printed and flexible electronics because it enables the deposition of functional metallic, semiconducting, and dielectric films with controlled thickness from tailored inks. Printing is also cost-effective because it simplifies processing and reduces infrastructure and logistical requirements. Printing is especially attractive for wearable devices because it can produce thin films on both rigid and flexible substrates. Although researchers have prepared MXene active layers using a wide variety of techniques, direct-write printing has shown considerable promise in recent studies. This spotlight article highlights recent advances in MXene applications in energy storage and harvesting, electromagnetic interference shielding, and antennas, along with background on ink formulation and thin-film fabrication using common printing methods.
articles.summary_en: This academic review examines direct-write printing of MXene active layers for scalable fabrication of thin-film devices. It covers applications in energy storage and harvesting, electromagnetic-interference shielding, antennas, and wearable electronics, alongside ink formulation and processing methods.

articles.title_original: Inkjet Printing of MXene Gas Sensors for Agricultural Monitoring
articles.title_en: Model-Guided Inkjet Printing Improves MXene Gas Sensor Fabrication
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Inkjet printing enables scalable fabrication of nanomaterial-based devices, but stable droplet formation and reproducible deposition remain challenging for emerging nanosheet inks. In this work, we develop a model-guided inkjet printing framework that monitors and optimizes droplet generation based on fluid properties and nozzle dynamics. Unlike previous MXene inkjet printing studies that primarily rely on empirical parameter tuning and focus on ink formulation or device performance, the proposed framework employs a physics-based analytical model that quantitatively links waveform parameters, fluid properties, nozzle dynamics, and droplet behavior. This predictive approach enables rational waveform design for stable single-droplet ejection, minimizes satellite droplet formation, and reduces the need for extensive experimental calibration. MXene (Ti3C2Tx) nanosheets dispersed in ethanol are used as a representative conductive ink to demonstrate the capability of the optimized printing approach. Under model-guided printing conditions, the system achieves reliable pattern formation and enables fabrication of printed MXene devices that exhibit measurable responses to several gases relevant to agricultural environments. These results demonstrate that analytical-model-guided monitoring and optimization of the inkjet printing process provides a predictive and generalizable strategy for reproducible printing of nanomaterial-based devices.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a physics-based framework to optimize droplet formation and deposition when inkjet printing Ti3C2Tx MXene nanosheet inks. The approach reduced satellite droplets, improved pattern reproducibility, and enabled gas sensors for agricultural monitoring.

articles.title_original: Beyond Conventional 2D Organic Semiconductors: Blade-Coated isoSiPc Thin Films with Tunable Crystalline Alignment for Organic Thin-Film Transistors
articles.title_en: Blade-Coated isoSiPc Films Enable Tunable Organic Transistors
articles.excerpt_original: Solution-processable two-dimensional organic single crystals (2D OSCs) have emerged as a highly promising class of materials for organic thin-film transistors (OTFTs), offering grain-boundary-free, long-range ordered active layers with exceptional charge transport properties. However, the current majority of 2D OSCs rely on planar, high-aspect-ratio, π-conjugated systems decorated in-plane with peripheral alkyl chains. Herein, we prepare 2D OSC-based OTFTs via blade coating of a recent material with a unique topology, isoSiPc, which combines a silicon phthalocyanine core with siloxane solubilizing chains that pass through the center of the π-conjugated core. We demonstrate that blade speed provides precise control over film morphology, crystallite texture, and in-plane alignment. Remarkably, we observe a blade-speed-dependent reorientation of crystallites within the film, directly correlating with device performance. At the optimal blade speed, an average hole mobility of 0.22 cm2V-1s-1 is achieved. Furthermore, application of our recently developed iodine post treatment enhances the average mobility to 0.44 cm2V-1s-1, with a champion device reaching 0.70 cm2V-1s-1. These results establish isoSiPc as a promising and structurally distinct 2D OSC platform, expanding the molecular design space and demonstrating a viable route toward high-performance, solution-processed organic electronics.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed solution-processed isoSiPc organic semiconductor films whose crystallite alignment and morphology can be controlled by blade-coating speed. Iodine treatment increased average hole mobility to 0.44 cm²/V·s, with a champion device reaching 0.70 cm²/V·s.

articles.title_original: Efficient transport kinetics of indirect excitons in van der Waals heterostructure
articles.title_en: Efficient Exciton Transport Observed in van der Waals Heterostructures
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Exciton transport is fundamental for understanding transport phenomena in bosonic systems and for exploring excitation energy transfer in materials. Spatially indirect excitons (IXs) have long lifetimes allowing them to form quantum bosonic states and travel long distances. Van der Waals heterostructures form a new materials platform for exploring IX transport. Disordered in-plane potentials suppress IX transport due to IX localization and scattering. In this work, we found the efficient IX transport kinetics characterized by anomalously high IX mobility. The efficient IX transport kinetics is observed in the presence of substantial in-plane disorder. The anomalously high IX mobility, its disappearance with increasing temperature, and its non-monotonic dependence on density are qualitatively consistent with theoretical predictions of IX superfluidity.
articles.summary_en: Researchers report anomalously high mobility of spatially indirect excitons despite substantial in-plane disorder. The results are consistent with theoretical predictions of exciton superfluidity, highlighting van der Waals heterostructures for studying energy transport in bosonic systems.

articles.title_en: Research Volume Examines Interface- and Defect-Engineered Nanomaterials
articles.excerpt_original: 《Nanomaterials at the Limit: Engineering Interfaces, Defects, Surfaces, and Programmable Matter》 is a flagship-scale research volume exploring what becomes possible when the properties of matter are no longer determined primarily by bulk composition, but by size, shape, surface, interface, defect structure, hierarchy, and nanoscale organization. The central question is: What kinds of materials can civilization design when structure itself becomes a controllable variable? At the nanoscale, matter behaves differently. Surface-to-volume ratio increases dramatically. Interfaces can dominate transport. Defects can become functional rather than merely undesirable. Quantum confinement can reshape electronic and optical behavior. Grain boundaries, pores, ligands, coatings, strain, topology, and local chemistry can alter macroscopic performance. This means that materials engineering begins to move beyond the traditional question: What is this material made of? and toward a deeper question: How is this material organized across multiple scales? The book develops this idea through the general framework: P_macro = F(d, shape, surface, interface, defect, composition, hierarchy) where macroscopic properties emerge from the coupled influence of nanoscale dimensions, morphology, interfaces, defects, chemistry, and hierarchical structure. This framework turns nanomaterials research into a broader design language. The objective is not simply to discover exotic nanoscale effects. It is to understand how those effects can be measured, stabilized, manufactured, reproduced, integrated, and eventually used in real systems. The book therefore introduces the Nano Functional Index: NFI = (Functional Gain_n × Stability_n × Scalability_n) / (1 + Defect Burden_n + Interface Loss_n + Criticality_n)
articles.summary_en: The volume discusses how nanoscale size, surfaces, interfaces, defects and hierarchical organization can be engineered to influence material properties. It proposes a general framework for assessing functional performance, stability and scalability, without identifying graphene-specific findings, companies or commercial applications.

articles.title_original: Performance-oriented pseudocapacitive energy storage of monovalent and divalent cation-driven Nb2CTx MXene electrodes
articles.title_en: Cation-intercalated Nb₂CTₓ MXenes boost pseudocapacitive storage
articles.excerpt_original: Restacking of two-dimensional materials, especially in MXene layers, hinders achieving potentially remarkable properties associated with these 2D nanosheets. In the MXene family, van der Waals and ionic restacking of Nb 2 CT x sheets mitigate their unique performance characteristics, rendering them an average performer compared to Ti-based MXenes. Herein, we propose the use of intercalating monovalent (Li 1+ , Na 1+ , and K 1+ ) and divalent (Mg 2+ ) ions to induce sheet separation, leading to high-performance Nb 2 CT x MXenes. Moreover, our findings highlight the understanding of the effect of various cation sizes on charge storage mechanisms and electrochemical characteristics in energy storage. The cation intercalation was performed via a self-electrostatic assembly method, which proves to be a simple, cost-effective, and scalable process. The effects of cation size on charge storage and electrochemical characteristics of MXenes for energy storage. The monovalent cation (K 1+ ) intercalated Nb 2 CT x MXene (870 F/g @ 5 mV/s) showed 6.85 times higher specific capacitance compared to pristine Nb 2 CT x MXene (127 F/g @ 5 mV/s). Moreover, the K +1 -Nb 2 CT x MXene posed low solution resistance (only ~0.23 Ω) and superior stability. In addition, the AC/K-Nb 2 CT x MXene device has demonstrated excellent power and energy density of 108 Wh/kg and 0.75 kW/kg at 1 A/g, respectively, making it a potential candidate for energy storage.
articles.summary_en: Researchers used Li⁺, Na⁺, K⁺, and Mg²⁺ intercalation to separate Nb₂CTₓ MXene sheets and improve charge storage. K⁺-intercalated electrodes reached 870 F/g, with an AC/K-Nb₂CTₓ device delivering 108 Wh/kg and 0.75 kW/kg, indicating potential for high-performance energy storage.

articles.title_original: MXene-Coated Hair Fibers as a Versatile Platform for Flexible Electronics, Intelligent Sensing, and Energy Harvesting
articles.title_en: MXene-Coated Hair Fibers Enable Humidity Sensing and Water-Evaporation Energy Harvesting
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Hair fibers with α-keratin biopolymers are responsive to water owing to the reversible disruption and formation of hydrogen bonds, which can be constructed as a hygrometer. However, the functionality is insufficient in smart sensors and energy harvesting because of their intrinsic insulation. Herein, electrically conductive hair fibers are produced by the layer-by-layer assembly method through forming MXene sheaths. Bovine serum albumin (BSA) with a positive charge is assembled firstly onto the hair fibers, and MXene nanosheets are adsorbed on the surface of the hair through electrostatic interactions. Due to the superior electrical conductivity of MXene and water responsivity of hair, hair fibers can be used in electric devices with enhanced mechanical properties and humidity sensitivity. The resultant fibers can be used as smart strain sensors with a high response speed (600 ms). More importantly, electric energy with a maximum output voltage of 97 mV can be achieved under water evaporation based on the transpiration-driven electrokinetic effect. Thus, this study not only extends fundamental knowledge about electrically conductive fiber but also develops an intriguing method to develop multifunctional hair fibers applicable in degradable wearable sensors and energy harvesting.
articles.summary_en: Researchers created electrically conductive hair fibers by coating bovine hair with MXene nanosheets using layer-by-layer assembly. The fibers function as fast strain and humidity sensors and generate up to 97 mV through water-evaporation-driven electrokinetic effects, indicating potential for degradable wearable devices.

articles.title_original: Synthesis of (Nb 1‐ y V y ) 4 C 3 T x Solid‐Solution MXenes and Their Supercapacitive Properties
articles.title_en: Solid-Solution MXenes Improve Supercapacitor Performance
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT MXene has attracted considerable attention as a highly promising electrode material owing to its exceptional electrochemical properties, mechanical flexibility, and tunable interfacial composition. Although M 4 C 3 ‐type MXenes are intrinsically more stable than their M 3 C 2 or M 2 C counterparts of identical M‐site chemistry, research to date has centered on Ti 3 C 2 T x and a handful of monometallic systems, leaving solid‐solution variants, especially M 4 C 3 configurations, scarcely investigated. Herein, we successfully fabricated a series of (Nb 1‐y V y ) 4 C 3 T x solid‐solution MXenes via controlled etching of corresponding MAX precursors. The incorporation of vanadium precisely regulates the surface terminal groups by reducing oxygen functional groups and increasing fluorine termination, which effectively modulates the ion transport and interfacial reaction kinetics. Benefiting from the optimized surface chemistry and solid‐solution synergy, the optimized (Nb 0.2 V 0.8 ) 4 C 3 T x electrode exhibits greatly improved rate capability and outstanding cycling stability, while the (Nb 0.4 V 0.6 ) 4 C 3 T x delivers the optimal specific capacitance. This work reveals the correlations among composition, surface chemistry, and electrochemical properties in M 4 C 3 ‐based solid‐solution MXenes, demonstrating that M‐site bimetallic solid‐solution engineering is an effective strategy to develop high‐performance MXene electrode materials.
articles.summary_en: Researchers synthesized (Nb₁₋ᵧVᵧ)₄C₃Tₓ solid-solution MXenes and linked vanadium content to surface termination, ion transport, and interfacial reaction kinetics. Optimized compositions showed improved rate capability, cycling stability, or specific capacitance, supporting bimetallic MXene engineering for supercapacitor electrodes.

articles.title_original: Anisotropic In-Plane Thermal Conductivity of Freestanding Few-Layer ReS2
articles.title_en: Few-Layer ReS₂ Shows Stacking-Dependent Anisotropic Thermal Conductivity
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract ReS2 is a low-symmetry transition-metal dichalcogenide exhibiting strong in-plane anisotropy, weak interlayer coupling, and stacking-dependent physical properties. While anisotropic thermal conductivity has been reported in bulk ReS2, experimental studies on stacking-dependent thermal conductivity and its thickness evolution in the few-layer regime remain largely unexplored. Here, we extract the thermal conductivity of freestanding, few-layer ReS2 samples (thickness <10 nm) using polarization-resolved optothermal Raman thermometry. All ReS2 samples show pronounced in-plane anisotropic thermal conductivity. Notably, the ∼3.5 nm AA-stacked flake shows higher thermal conductivity than the AB-stacked flake of the same thickness, highlighting the influence of stacking order on phonon transport. The in-plane thermal conductivity displays a nonmonotonic dependence on thickness over the ∼2.5–8 nm range, which is supported by density functional theory calculations. These findings provide key insight into anisotropic phonon transport in low-symmetry 2D materials and highlight the potential of few-layer ReS2 for nanoscale thermal management and thermoelectric applications.
articles.summary_en: Researchers measured strong in-plane thermal-conductivity anisotropy in freestanding few-layer ReS₂ using polarization-resolved optothermal Raman thermometry. Conductivity varied nonmonotonically with thickness and was higher in an AA-stacked flake than an equivalent AB-stacked flake, informing nanoscale thermal-management and thermoelectric applications.

articles.title_original: High-sensitivity deep shortwave infrared organic photodetectors enabled by selenium-integrated quinoidal molecular semiconductor
articles.title_en: Selenium-integrated organic photodetectors extend deep-SWIR sensitivity
articles.excerpt_original: Developing organic photodetectors (OPDs) that can detect in deep shortwave infrared (deep-SWIR) region (1.2–1.6 μm) is technologically important. Yet, the performance of the state-of-the-art deep-SWIR OPDs remains substantially limited. Herein, we report a selenium-integrated quinoidal small molecular acceptor, SeBz-4Cl, enabling highly sensitive deep-SWIR photodetection. Selenium incorporation enhances quinoidal character along the conjugated backbone of the molecules, thus expanding absorption approaching 1.5 μm. Moreover, SeBz-4Cl with strengthened intermolecular interactions led to an ideal film morphology, which reduced Urbach energy and favored charge dynamics. Under −1 V voltage bias, the SeBz-4Cl-based OPD achieved a low dark current density of 2.97 × 10−7 A cm−2 and an external quantum efficiency (EQE) of 7.8% at 1310 nm, together with a high specific detectivity (D*) exceeding 1011 Jones across 500–1400 nm, representing advanced deep-SWIR OPD performance. Furthermore, an optical communication system and a flexible imager under 1.2 μm illumination were demonstrated, highlighting potential of these deep-SWIR OPDs for information electronics and next generation optoelectronic applications in future. Organic photodetectors for deep shortwave infrared light remain limited in sensitivity and spectral reach. Wei et al. developed a selenium-integrated molecule with a high specific detectivity exceeding 1011 Jones across 500–1400 nm, which enables flexible imaging and optical communication.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a selenium-integrated quinoidal molecular semiconductor for deep shortwave-infrared organic photodetectors, achieving detectivity above 10¹¹ Jones across 500–1400 nm and 7.8% EQE at 1310 nm. Demonstrations in optical communications and flexible imaging indicate potential for advanced optoelectronic and flexible sensing applications.

articles.title_en: Perforated MXene Structures Show Tunable Auxeticity

articles.title_original: Electrical signal transmission across electrolyte junctions separated by atomically-thin graphene
articles.title_en: Atomically Thin Graphene Transmits Electrical Signals Across Electrolyte Junctions
articles.excerpt_original: Signal transmission across membranes is usually mediated by the permeation of molecular species. Here we show that atomically thin graphene crystals, although impermeable to any ions or molecules, can transmit interfacial electrical potentials across electrolyte junctions without significant disruption. In monolayer graphene, applying an electrical potential at one graphene-electrolyte interface induces a similar responsive potential at the opposite side, with the magnitude governed by ionic sizes. By increasing the number of graphene layers, the response decays and vanishes at ~ 5 layers. Theoretical analysis attributes these observations to graphene’s tunable charge-carrier concentration combined with its extreme thinness. This capability of transmitting activation stimuli without mass transport may find its applications in artificial synapses and other neuromorphic junctions. This study shows that atomically thin graphene can transmit electrical signals between separated liquids without allowing ions or molecules to pass, enabling communication across otherwise impermeable membranes.
articles.summary_en: Researchers show that monolayer graphene can transmit interfacial electrical potentials between separated electrolytes while blocking ions and molecules. The response depends on ionic size and disappears at roughly five graphene layers, suggesting applications in artificial synapses and neuromorphic devices.

articles.title_original: Iridium Nanoparticles Anchored on Reduced Graphene Oxide for Efficient Photoelectrochemical Photodetection
articles.title_en: Iridium nanoparticles on reduced graphene oxide improve photoelectrochemical photodetection
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Despite the extensive and mature research on iridium (Ir) complexes for electro-to-light conversion, there is a striking imbalance in Ir-based optoelectronic materials for light-to-electricity conversion, particularly high-performance photodetectors, which have rarely been investigated. In this study, Ir nanoparticles (NPs) were loaded onto reduced graphene oxide (rGO), abbreviated as Ir NP/rGO, using commercial tris(2-(4,6-difluorophenyl)pyridine) iridium(III) and graphene oxide (GO) via hydrogen bonding interaction, followed by vacuum calcination, for the first time, for the construction of a photoelectrochemical (PEC)-type photodetector. The PEC result demonstrates that the as-obtained Ir NP/rGO-based PEC electrode shows the best PEC signal (e.g., current density and responsivity) at the smallest diameter of studied It NPs that were calcinated at the lowest temperature (600 °C). The current density and responsivity for the Ir NP/rGO-based PEC electrode in 0.5 M KOH can reach 34.7 μA cm−2 and 294 μA W−1, respectively, both of which are remarkably higher than those of emerging nanostructure-based PEC electrodes. Moreover, the Ir NP/rGO-based PEC electrode achieves competitive detectivity, comparable response/recovery time, as well as robust PEC stability. It is anticipated that Ir-based nanostructures can offer promising avenues for the rational design of high-efficiency, stable optoelectronic devices, including photodetectors, PEC sensors, and optoelectronic switches.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed an iridium nanoparticle/reduced graphene oxide electrode for photoelectrochemical photodetection. The electrode achieved a reported current density of 34.7 μA cm⁻² and responsivity of 294 μA W⁻¹ in 0.5 M KOH, alongside competitive detectivity, response/recovery times, and stability.

articles.title_original: NanoMatAI: band gaps of 2D semiconductors from crystal structure, with a calibrated trust verdict
articles.title_en: NanoMatAI Predicts 2D Semiconductor Band Gaps with Calibrated Reliability
articles.excerpt_original: A CGCNN ensemble that predicts the band gap of a two-dimensional monolayer from its crystal structure on CPU, together with a calibrated uncertainty interval and an explicit verdict on whether the prediction is usable. Trained on 22 103 PBE monolayers — stable and metastable Alexandria entries and non-magnetic 2DMatPedia ones — and evaluated on a split where no composition is shared between training and test: MAE 0.225 eV, against 0.430 eV for a composition-only baseline scored on the identical test set. The graph reads bond angles as well as bond lengths, which is what lets it separate polymorphs of one composition — 1H-MoS2 is a semiconductor and 1T-MoS2 is metallic, and a distance-only graph barely tells them apart. Three independent out-of-domain checks decide the verdict: a metal/semiconductor gate, the spread between ensemble members, and the distance to the training set in the model's own latent space. Each exists because the previous one was caught failing on a real case. The 90% interval is calibrated per cell of ensemble spread and of resemblance to the metastable population, which a linear head on the latent space detects at ROC-AUC 0.85; on structures the model never trained on it covers 88%. Linear heads on that latent space add a quasiparticle gap, an exciton binding energy and an absorption onset; a second ensemble adds the work function, so the band edges a contact metal is chosen on follow from the pair. Predictions for 28 372 public 2D structures are published as a browsable static page, with a periodic-table map of where the model actually works, and an MCP server exposes the tool, verdict first, to language models.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a crystal-structure-based CGCNN ensemble that predicts band gaps in 2D monolayers with a reported 0.225 eV MAE, outperforming a composition-only baseline. Its uncertainty estimates, out-of-domain checks and published predictions for 28,372 structures aim to improve the reliability of computational screening and contact-metal selection.

articles.title_original: Tungsten‐Boosted Erbium Oxide–Graphene Nanoplatelet Electrode for Voltammetric Determination of Metaproterenol
articles.title_en: Tungsten–Erbium Oxide–Graphene Electrode Enables Sensitive Metaproterenol Detection
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT In this study, an electrochemical sensor was developed by modifying a glassy carbon electrode (GCE) with a nanostructured composite of graphene nanoplatelets (GNPs), ultrasound‐assisted synthesized erbium oxide (Er 2 O 3 ), and tungsten (W) nanoparticles. The platform (W@Er 2 O 3 ‐GNPs/GCE) exhibited favorable electrochemical characteristics, including a relatively low charge transfer resistance (Rct = 136 Ω) and an enlarged electroactive surface area (A = 0.227 cm 2 ). The modified electrode exhibited enhanced electrocatalytic activity toward the oxidation of metaproterenol, as evidenced by the increased oxidation peak current and the shift of the oxidation peak potential (Epa) toward less positive potentials. This enhanced performance is attributed to the complementary contributions of GNPs, which provide a high‐surface‐area conductive framework, and Er 2 O 3 @W nanoparticles, which provide additional electroactive sites and favorable interfacial properties for the oxidation of metaproterenol. The developed platform exhibited a linear working range of 2.4 × 10 −7 –1.4 × 10 −5 M, an analytical sensitivity of 0.5732 µA µM −1 , and a low detection limit of 3.0 × 10 −8 M. The proposed method also demonstrated repeatability with an RSD < 1.5% over 10 scans, storage stability with a signal loss <4.0% after 15 days of storage, and satisfactory recoveries in complex media.
