articles.title_original: High-Carrier Mobility Screening of Polar Multivalley Two-Dimensional Alkaline Earth Monohalides
articles.title_en: Screening identifies CaI and SrI as high-mobility 2D semiconductor candidates
articles.excerpt_original: High carrier mobility in two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors is critical for next-generation electronics, yet identifying promising candidates remains challenging owing to multiple competing scattering mechanisms and the substantial computational expense of rigorous transport evaluation. Here, we generalize a symmetry-restoring deformation potential approximation formalism by accounting for multi-valley degeneracy, and present a hierarchical screening workflow integrating this formalism with rigorous Wannier-interpolated ab initio electron-phonon coupling calculations to accurately evaluate 2D materials for superior transport. Applying this screening workflow to the alkaline-earth metal monohalide family, the deformation potential approximation approach initially identifies these halides as promising candidates with optimistic mobility upper bounds of 102-104 cm2 V −1 s −1 . Advancing rigorous electron-phonon coupling calculations to capture the decisive limiting role of polar optical phonons, we highlight monolayers CaI (μe ≈ 180,μℎ ≈ 93 cm2 V −1 s −1 ) and SrI (μe ≈ 270, μℎ ≈ 149 cm2 V −1 s −1 ) as robust candidates. This resilience is attributed to a synergistic interplay of small effective mass and large dielectric screening. This work establishes a reproducible framework for the precise evaluation of polar 2D semiconductors.
articles.summary_en: A hierarchical workflow combining deformation-potential screening with rigorous electron–phonon calculations identifies monolayer CaI and SrI as promising polar 2D semiconductors. Their predicted electron mobilities reach approximately 180 and 270 cm² V⁻¹ s⁻¹, respectively, with dielectric screening and low effective mass limiting scattering effects.

articles.title_original: Theory of optical alignment and orientation of excitons in an ensemble of semiconductor nanoplatelets
articles.title_en: Theory of Exciton Optical Alignment in Semiconductor Nanoplatelet Ensembles
articles.excerpt_original: We present the theory of exciton optical alignment and optical orientation effects in a single semiconductor nanoplatelet (NPL) and in an ensemble of NPLs. The theoretical model is developed to take into account the emission from both bright and dark exciton states in the case of strong electron-hole exchange interaction and an isotropic distribution of in-plane orientations of the NPLs' edges with respect to the linear polarization axis. The conditions for the linear optical response regime on the polarized resonant excitation of the bright exciton are considered, and the steady-state and time-dependent expressions for polarized photoluminescence are presented for the low temperature case in the Faraday magnetic field at normal incidence. The symmetry of the obtained optical response corresponds to the $C_{2}$ point group for the single NPL and the $C_{\infty}$ point group for the NPL ensemble. The bright-to-dark exciton coupling mechanism allowing one to observe the optical alignment of the dark exciton is considered. The example calculations of the effects are presented for the parameters close to those of CdSe/CdS core/shell NPLs. The effect of the fluctuations in the exciton parameters in the ensemble on the polarization dephasing in the transverse effective magnetic field is demonstrated.
articles.summary_en: Researchers develop a theoretical model describing optical alignment and orientation of bright and dark excitons in individual semiconductor nanoplatelets and ensembles. The analysis models polarized photoluminescence, symmetry effects, and dephasing, with parameters relevant to CdSe/CdS core–shell nanoplatelets.

articles.title_original: Berry curvature dipole generation and nonreciprocal spin photocurrents in ferroelectricity polarized heterostructures
articles.title_en: Ferroelectric heterostructures generate Berry curvature dipoles in multilayer WSe2
articles.excerpt_original: Berry curvature dipole (BCD) describes the dipole-like distribution of Berry curvature in momentum space and plays a key role for quantum geometric phenomena in nonlinear optoelectronics. Experimentally, BCD can be generated at artificially designed semiconductor heterointerfaces where rotational symmetry breaking is induced by interfacial lattice mismatch. Such a local interface symmetry breaking strategy is largely limited to the monolayer regime; however, how to induce BCD in thicker semiconductors remains challenging. Here, we demonstrate a strategy for BCD generation in semiconductors beyond the monolayer limit via ferroelectric-polarization-driven symmetry breaking in WSe2/LiNbO3 heterostructures. In contrast to the absence of circular galvanic photocurrent under normal incidence due to the C3 symmetry in WSe2, the in-plane polarization of LiNbO3 in heterostructures breaks the C3 symmetry of WSe2 multilayers into Cs or C1, and induces pronounced circular galvanic photocurrents therein. Importantly, such galvanic photocurrent is nonreciprocal to bias voltage with a giant asymmetry factor of 12. First-principles calculations reveal that the symmetry breaking and energy band reconstruction in multilayer WSe2 induced by polarization field gives rise to a strongly-anisotropic Berry curvature distribution and further generates BCD. Our results on ferroelectricity-driven BCD provide a strategy for engineering quantum geometry in nonlinear optoelectronic devices. Berry curvature dipole (BCD) in 2D materials originates from rotational symmetry breaking and can generate quantum nonlinear optoelectronic phenomena. Here, the authors demonstrate a strategy for BCD and circular photogalvanic effect generation in semiconductors beyond the monolayer limit via ferroelectric-polari
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrated polarization-driven symmetry breaking in WSe2/LiNbO3 heterostructures, generating Berry curvature dipoles and circular photocurrents beyond the monolayer limit. The effect produced strongly nonreciprocal photocurrents, pointing to potential nonlinear optoelectronic applications.

articles.title_original: Dimensionality-driven functional properties of bulk and two-dimensional alkaline-earth tellurides: A DFT based investigations
articles.title_en: DFT Study Finds Distinct Properties in Bulk and 2D Alkaline-Earth Tellurides
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Bulk semiconductors possess an abundance of new scientific knowledge from the development of two-dimensional (2D) materials by modifying the quantum mechanical behaviour of the semiconductors. This study reports on the detailed first-principles computations of alkaline-earth tellurides with a rocksalt (NaCl type) structure, i.e., bulk (3D) structures CaTe, SrTe, and BaTe and their corresponding 2D monolayers. The density functional theory (DFT) approach is used for these calculations, employing full-potential linearized augmented plane wave (FP-LAPW) methods from the WIEN2k package. Structural relaxations are performed with the Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof generalized gradient approximation (PBE-GGA) functional, whereas band gaps are computed using the modified Becke-Johnson potential of Tran-Blaha (TB-mBJ) for the bulk structures and the local modified Becke-Johnson potential (LmBJ) for the 2D monolayers. It is observed that all three 2D monolayers are dynamically and mechanically stable due to the absence of imaginary modes and agreement with the Born-Huang stability criteria for the phonon dispersion. The bulk compounds have indirect-gaps (Eg = 2.15–2.47 eV), whereas the monolayers exhibit direct gaps at Γ (2.46–2.85 eV). This dimensionality reduction results in a significant modification in the optical properties also. Static dielectric constants, refractive indices, and reflectivity values decrease approximately 67%, 42%, and 87%, respectively, decreasing the static dielectric response of the monolayers relative to the bulk compounds with absorption onset in the visible (2.46-2.85 eV, ~435-505 nm). The thermoelectric analysis shows a significant level of Seebeck coefficients. The 3D bulk tellurides and monolayers of CaTe/SrTe are the examples of materials with p
articles.summary_en: Researchers used first-principles calculations to compare bulk and monolayer CaTe, SrTe, and BaTe. The 2D materials were predicted to be stable, exhibit direct band gaps in the visible range, and show substantially reduced dielectric, refractive, and reflectivity responses versus bulk forms.

articles.title_original: Interlayer Mismatch and Solvated Intermediates Control Spacer Mixing in 2D Perovskites
articles.title_en: Spacer mismatch governs structure in mixed 2D perovskites
articles.excerpt_original: Organic spacer mixing is a versatile strategy for tuning the structure and properties of two-dimensional layered halide perovskites (2DLHPs), yet the factors that govern the resulting mixing configuration remain poorly understood. Here we investigate mixtures of alkyl monoammonium Ruddlesden–Popper (RP) and alkyl diammonium Dion–Jacobson (DJ) 2DLHPs and identify three structural outcomes: alloying, phase separation, and superlattice formation. Across twenty spacer combinations, the interlayer-spacing mismatch between the parent perovskites largely determines the outcome, with small mismatch favoring alloys and large mismatch favoring phase separation. A superlattice phase with a period exceeding either parent, consistent with alternating RP and DJ layers, forms only at large mismatch and only for blends containing 1,4-butanediammonium (DC4). In situ absorption spectroscopy and single-crystal structure determination reveal that superlattice formation proceeds through a dimethylformamide (DMF)-containing intermediate in which DC4 and n-pentylammonium (C5) occupy distinct bridging and intercalated crystallographic sites, producing an ordered precursor that converts to the superlattice upon annealing. Structural mismatch and intermediate-phase chemistry together govern alloying, phase separation, and superlattice formation in mixed-spacer 2DLHPs.
articles.summary_en: Researchers found that interlayer-spacing mismatch largely determines whether mixed 2D halide perovskites form alloys, phase-separated structures, or superlattices. Solvated intermediates involving DMF and specific spacer molecules help drive ordered superlattice formation during annealing.

articles.title_original: Introduction to TFET design and simulation
articles.title_en: Introduction to TFET Design and Simulation
articles.excerpt_original: This chapter describes the history and future research work for the design and development of semiconductor transistors. Technology Computer-Aided Design (TCAD)-based transistor design helps in designing performance optimization with the help of material selection for channel, source, drain, gate, and oxide region under different bias conditions. It also provides support for process temperature and voltage variation impact on transistor designs. The important parameters of transistor design are channel potential, electric field, subthreshold conduction, leakage current, threshold voltage, gate capacitance, and transconductance. TCAD helps in the design and simulation of both 2D and 3D transistors.
articles.summary_en: This academic chapter reviews the history and future development of tunnel field-effect transistors (TFETs). It highlights TCAD-based optimization of materials and device regions, alongside key performance parameters including leakage, threshold voltage, electric field, and transconductance.

articles.title_original: Finite element Dirac-like equation solver for graphene
articles.title_en: Finite-element solver models electronic states in graphene quantum dots
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract We present a finite-element formulation for solving the Dirac-like equation governing electronic states in graphene quantum dots (GQDs). The two-component Dirac equation reduces to a scalar equation in divergence form for the A -sublattice amplitude, which we discretise by the standard Galerkin method. The domain is truncated at a finite outer radius with an open boundary condition that allows outgoing wave solutions. Using the linear Dirac dispersion E = ℏ v F k , the resulting quadratic eigenvalue problem in E is converted as a quadratic polynomial eigenvalue problem in the wavenumber k and solved with scalable Library for Eigenvalue Problem Computations. As a test case, we compare against the scanning tunnelling spectroscopy of Gutiérrez et al on a 2.75 nm GQD on Cu(111). The solver recovers the first three resonance energies to within 1 − 10 meV of the analytical Dirac calculation reported in that work and 11 − 35 meV of the measured peak positions, and reproduces the angular-momentum-resolved wavefunction structure.
articles.summary_en: Researchers present a scalable finite-element solver for the Dirac-like equation governing graphene quantum dots. Validated against analytical calculations and scanning-tunnelling spectroscopy, it reproduces resonance energies and angular-momentum-resolved wavefunctions with close agreement.

articles.title_original: A unified model for the thermal and electrical conductivities of highly oriented graphene–ceramic matrix composites
articles.title_en: Unified Model Predicts Conductivity in Oriented Graphene–Ceramic Composites
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Ceramic matrix composites serve as crucial structural materials for hot-section components in next-generation aeroengines and aerospace propulsion systems. As functional reinforcements, graphene fillers have been introduced into ceramic matrices to form graphene–ceramic matrix composites (GCMCs), with the potential for enhanced thermal and electrical properties. In such composites, interfacial effects and graphene orientation are important influencing factors. Pressure-assisted sintering induces highly oriented graphene alignment that can be described by Gaussian distribution, leading to complex predictive formulations. Thus, this study proposes a unified theoretical model to evaluate the anisotropic thermal and electrical conductivities of GCMCs. For the orientation distribution of graphene fillers, an equivalent relation between the parameters of a Gaussian distribution and those of a uniform distribution within a finite angle range is established, enabling accurate predictions using a simplified formulation. Two categories of interfacial effects are considered, including Kapitza and contact thermal resistances for heat conduction and the tunneling effect for electrical conduction. The enhancements of thermal and electrical conductivities differ with graphene addition due to different interfacial effects, accompanied by contrasting anisotropy evolutions. Electrical anisotropy tends to stabilize after percolation, whereas thermal anisotropy evolves continuously with increasing graphene volume fraction.
articles.summary_en: Researchers propose a theoretical model for anisotropic thermal and electrical conductivity in highly oriented graphene–ceramic matrix composites produced by pressure-assisted sintering. The work accounts for graphene orientation, interfacial thermal resistances and electrical tunneling, supporting design of multifunctional materials for aerospace hot-section applications.

articles.title_original: Interfacial Z-Scheme Heterostructure in Porous MXene-Fe3O4@Ag Nanocomposites toward Doxycycline Disintegration
articles.title_en: MXene–Fe3O4@Ag nanocomposite enables solar doxycycline degradation
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Nanoscale electronic structure at heterointerfaces critically governs charge-transfer pathways and photocatalytic efficiency, yet direct experimental insight remains limited. Herein, we report an interfacial Z-scheme heterostructure in a porous MXene-Fe3O4@Ag nanocomposite, allowing direct resolution and correlation of nanoscale electronic properties with efficient doxycycline disintegration under ambient solar irradiation. Hybrid integration of plasmonic Ag and magnetic Fe3O4 nanoparticles onto conductive Ti3C2 MXene sheets generates densely coupled heterointerfaces with pronounced electronic reconstruction. Scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy, complemented by Kelvin probe force microscopy, reveal local density-of-states modulation and nanoscale band bending at the MXene-Fe3O4@Ag junctions before and after illumination, while X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy confirms interfacial charge redistribution. Together, these experimental observations provide direct evidence for a Z-scheme charge-transfer architecture. Enabled by this optimized interfacial electronic landscape, the nanocomposite achieves complete doxycycline disintegration with a substantially enhanced apparent quantum yield and significantly reduced solar energy consumption. The photocatalytic performance remains robust in complex real water matrices, including tap water, river water, and wastewater. Reactive species trapping experiments identify •OH radicals as the dominant oxidative species, elucidating the Z-scheme-driven photocatalytic mechanism. This study establishes nanoscale electronic-structure engineering as a key design principle for MXene-based Z-scheme photocatalysts for sustainable pharmaceutical wastewater remediation.
articles.summary_en: Researchers resolved Z-scheme charge-transfer behavior in a porous MXene–Fe3O4@Ag nanocomposite using nanoscale electronic-structure measurements. The photocatalyst completely degraded doxycycline under ambient solar irradiation and remained effective in tap water, river water, and wastewater, indicating potential for pharmaceutical wastewater remediation.

articles.title_original: Chasing Bose‐Einstein and Maxwell‐Boltzmann Distributions of Exciton‐Polaritons in a 2D Semiconductor Microcavity
articles.title_en: Temperature-Tunable Exciton-Polariton Distributions Demonstrated in a 2D Semiconductor Microcavity
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Exciton polaritons (EPs) in two‐dimensional (2D) semiconductor microcavities have emerged as an attractive platform for high‐temperature polaritonic optoelectronics, owing to large exciton binding energies and superior thermal stability of transition‐metal dichalcogenides. Manipulating EP populations is crucial for understanding bosonic thermodynamics and developing tunable polaritonic devices. Most polariton devices employ lower‐polariton (LP) emission; by contrast, strong upper‐polariton (UP) emission remains a challenging yet highly desired counterpart for realizing controllable UP‐LP emitters. Here, we demonstrate tunable emission from primary LPs to robust UPs in a 2D semiconductor microcavity, revealing crossovers in polariton probability distributions between Bose‐Einstein (BE) and Maxwell‐Boltzmann (MB) statistics at elevated temperatures. Temperature‐dependent excitonic band renormalization and photonic cavity shrinkage lead to a reversal of the exciton‐photon detuning from negative to positive, reconstructing excitonic and photonic fractions in the formed EPs. At 318 K, the LP and UP populations follow BE and MB distributions, respectively. However, their statistical distributions are reversed at 378 K, where the thermal excitation assists the accumulation of the UP population and favors the BE distribution. Our findings provide insights into the basic thermodynamics of polaritonic populations, establishing a practical route to develop tunable LP‐UP devices.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrated tunable lower- and upper-polariton emission and observed temperature-dependent crossover between Bose–Einstein and Maxwell–Boltzmann distributions at 318–378 K. The findings support development of tunable polaritonic optoelectronic devices based on 2D semiconductors.

articles.title_original: High-Pressure Investigation of 2D van der Waals Layered Ferromagnet Cr1.28Te2
articles.title_en: Pressure Tunes Structural, Electrical, and Magnetic States in Cr1.28Te2
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Cr1+δTe2, a family among two-dimensional (2D) van der Waals (vdW) transition-metal dichalcogenides, has garnered significant interest owing to its tunable structural, electrical, and magnetic properties controlled by the concentration of self-intercalated Cr atoms. Among various external stimuli, pressure provides an additional route to tune the associated physical properties of these materials through modifications of interatomic distances, which can substantially alter the electrical and magnetic properties. In the present study, we report the theoretical and experimental investigation of the pressure-induced structural and electrical properties of Cr1.28Te2 with trigonal (P3̅m1) crystal structure. The pressure-dependent synchrotron X-ray powder diffraction (SXRPD) analysis revealed iso-structural transitions at ∼4.7, ∼9.9, and ∼19.7 GPa, evidenced by the deviation of lattice parameters from linear pressure dependence. The temperature-dependent resistance curves measured over a range of applied pressure show the presence of metal-semiconductor-metal transition near ∼7.8 and ∼16.8 GPa, close to the pressures of the iso-structural transitions. Additionally, a low-temperature resistance minimum observed at low pressures suggests the emergence of localization-related effects. The resistance minimum gradually shifts toward higher temperatures with increasing pressure, indicating the progressive enhancement of localization effect under compression. Further, theoretical calculations suggest that the metallic nature of Cr1.28Te2 below the metal-semiconductor transition (i.e., at low pressure) is dominated by Cr2–3d states, whereas above the transition (at high pressure), the metallicity is governed by Te–3p states. A nonmonotonic evolution of the magnetic state is al
articles.summary_en: Researchers experimentally and theoretically investigated pressure-driven changes in layered ferromagnetic Cr1.28Te2. Synchrotron diffraction and resistance measurements identified multiple structural transitions and metal–semiconductor–metal behavior at pressures up to approximately 20 GPa.

articles.title_original: 基于Fe3GaTe2/WSe2/Fe3GaTe2范德华异质结构的自旋阀效应研究
articles.title_en: All-2D Fe3GaTe2/WSe2 Heterostructure Demonstrates Spin-Valve Effect
articles.excerpt_original: Spin valves are core components in spintronics, widely used in magnetic memory and sensing. To advance the miniaturization and low power consumption of 2D spintronic devices, this study systematically investigates the magnetotransport properties of a fully 2D van der Waals spin valve heterostructure based on ferromagnetic Fe3GaTe2 and semiconductor WSe2. Fe3GaTe2 single crystals were synthesized via a high-temperature self-flux technique, and their excellent crystalline quality and uniform elemental distribution were confirmed by Raman spectroscopy, XRD, XPS, and EDS. Subsequently, the Fe3GaTe2/WSe2/Fe3GaTe2 vertical heterostructure was fabricated using mechanical exfoliation and dry transfer techniques, and its transport properties were evaluated in a physical property measurement system. Experimental results demonstrate that the heterojunction shows a strictly linear I-V response at 250 K, establishing an excellent Ohmic contact. Under an out-of-plane magnetic field, the device exhibits a distinct step-like magnetoresistance curve at 250 K, firmly confirming the spin valve effect. Furthermore, the magnetoresistance ratio decays significantly as the bias current increases from 1 nA to 1 μA, and remains highly constant over a 360° range when the direction of the applied magnetic field is varied at 250 K, demonstrating a completely angular-independent characteristic. This unique isotropic transport behavior originates from the intrinsic strong perpendicular magnetic anisotropy of Fe3GaTe2. This study verifies the feasibility of achieving spin valve modulation in all 2D systems and provides a solid physical basis for constructing magnetic angular-insensitive spin transport devices.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrated spin-valve behavior in a vertical Fe3GaTe2/WSe2/Fe3GaTe2 van der Waals heterostructure, with step-like magnetoresistance at 250 K. The device showed angle-independent transport, supporting development of miniaturized, low-power spintronic memory and sensing technologies.

articles.title_original: A Comprehensive Route for Safe and Sustainable Graphene Oxide Synthesis
articles.title_en: Safer, More Sustainable Route for Graphene Oxide Synthesis
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract For almost sixty years, the modified Hummers method has been used to oxidise graphite with the radicals of KMnO 4 (MnO 3+ ) to produce graphene oxide (GO) with the use of H 2 O 2 as a terminating chemical in the reaction. NaNO₃ has traditionally been employed as a catalyst in the Hummers method, but its use is associated with the release of toxic byproducts such as NO₂ and N₂O₄. Moreover, recent studies have shown that excessive H₂O₂ can reduce GO, rendering it hydrophobic and causing partial precipitation. In this study, we propose a variation to the conventional method by reducing the dosage of NaNO₃ and eliminating the use of H₂O₂. This approach is experimentally evaluated and compared with conventional protocols that employ both NaNO 3 and H₂O₂. The results highlight that minimising NaNO 3 avoids the high risk of releasing hazardous NOₓ species, and H 2 O 2 -free reaction helps to obtain more stable rGO (a high-quality colloidal dispersion with chemical modification). The colloidal solution retains its stability for up to three months for rGO suspension.
articles.summary_en: Researchers propose modifying the Hummers method by reducing sodium nitrate and eliminating hydrogen peroxide. The approach aims to reduce hazardous nitrogen oxide emissions while producing a stable reduced graphene oxide colloidal suspension for up to three months.

articles.title_original: Features of Thermal behavior of Nanocrystalline Ceria in the Presence of Oxygen-Free Graphene
articles.title_en: Oxygen-Free Graphene Lowers Ceria Sintering Temperature
articles.excerpt_original: A comparative study of the morphology, phase composition, and thermal behavior of nanocrystalline ceria powder and graphene-containing composites based on it, which were synthesized using two methods combining sol-gel and sonochemical techniques, has been carried out. In one case, ceria crystallization occurred on the oxygen-free graphene sheets as a result of the interaction of Ce-containing sol and few-layer graphene suspension in an N,N-dimethyloctylamine-aqua emulsion. In another case, the graphene sheets were deposited on ceria nanocrystallites by combining the suspensions of ceria and graphene in an isopropanol-aqua mixture. It was found that the introduction of less than 1 wt % graphene leads to a decrease in the sintering temperature of nanocrystalline ceria by 175°C if the composite was obtained from a Ce-containing sol, and by 212°C if a nanocrystallite ceria was used for this purpose. The shapes of the shrinkage curves and shrinkage rates of composites also differ, and in both cases there are significant differences from the data for pure nanocrystallite ceria obtained under the same conditions.
articles.summary_en: Researchers found that adding less than 1 wt% oxygen-free graphene to nanocrystalline ceria reduced its sintering temperature by 175–212°C, depending on the synthesis route. The graphene–ceria composites also showed distinct shrinkage behavior compared with pure ceria, indicating potential value for thermal processing and ceramic composite design.

articles.title_original: Ultrasound-assisted liquid phase exfoliation of graphite: Statistical optimization of graphene dispersion quality
articles.title_en: Statistical optimization improves ultrasound-assisted graphene exfoliation
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Graphene, a crystalline allotrope of carbon, has garnered significant attention in the scientific community due to its exceptional properties, such as high electrical conductivity, mechanical strength, and flexibility. These characteristics enable a wide range of applications in fields such as electronics, composite materials, and biomedicine. Among the various methods for producing graphene, Liquid Phase Exfoliation (LPE) is considered highly advantageous, as it allows for the creation of dispersions with high concentration and few layers, which are essential for maximizing the material's properties. In this study, Response Surface Methodology (RSM) was employed to investigate the impact of key parameters in the LPE process, including sonication time, type of graphite used, centrifugation time, and centrifugation speed. UV-Vis spectroscopy was applied to analyze the dispersions, enabling the characterization of the obtained graphene. Parameter optimization was conducted through Analysis of Variance (ANOVA), resulting in the definition of optimal conditions for graphene production. This study highlights the effectiveness of the LPE process in producing high-quality graphene, as well as its potential applications in enhancing polymer composites, underscoring the relevance of this material in the development of new technologies.
articles.summary_en: Researchers optimized liquid-phase exfoliation of graphite using sonication, graphite type, centrifugation time and speed. The resulting graphene dispersions were characterized by UV–Vis spectroscopy, with potential use in polymer composites.

articles.title_original: Lateral Size-Controlled Sulfur-Doped Graphene Aerogels with Tunable Electrical and Magnetic Properties
articles.title_en: Sulfur-Doped Graphene Aerogels Show Size-Dependent Electrical and Magnetic Properties
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Graphene aerogel, an ultralight and highly porous material, shows promise for applications including energy storage, environmental sustainability, electronics, and biomedical fields. The roles of the lateral sheet size and heteroatom doping in graphene are key to its properties. In this study, we examine the combined effect of lateral size and sulfur (S) doping on the electrical and magnetic properties of reduced graphene oxide aerogel (rGA). A sonication-assisted method is used to control the lateral size of graphene oxide (GO) sheets: large-lateral-size GO (GO1) and small-lateral-size GO (GO2). The rGA is synthesized using a hydrothermal-assisted self-assembly process and characterized by X-ray diffraction (XRD), Raman spectroscopy, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), and field-emission scanning electron microscopy (FESEM). The electrical conductivity of rGA1 increases ∼114% after S-doping at 1.44 at.%, while for rGA2, it rises ∼74% at an S-doping of 2.10 at.%. Both S-doped rGA1 and rGA2 show diamagnetic behavior at room temperature (RT) and show temperature-dependent magnetic responses. The mass magnetization of both S-doped rGA1 and rGA2 improves by ∼213% and ∼81%, respectively, at RT. These results indicate that variations in lateral size and S-doping greatly affect the structural, electrical, and magnetic properties of graphene aerogels.
articles.summary_en: Researchers controlled graphene oxide sheet size and sulfur doping in reduced graphene oxide aerogels, finding substantial increases in electrical conductivity and room-temperature mass magnetization. The results clarify how structural dimensions and heteroatom doping tune aerogel properties, but no specific commercial application was demonstrated.

articles.title_original: Harnessing the Potential of 2D Ti3C2 MXene: A First-Principles Study on Structural, Electronic, Optical, and Mechanical Properties
articles.title_en: First-Principles Study Maps Ti3C2 MXene Properties for Electronic Applications
articles.excerpt_original: In this study, we employ first-principles density functional theory (DFT) calculations using the CASTEP framework to investigate the structural, electronic, mechanical, and optical properties of the two-dimensional (2D) Ti3C2 MXene material. The optimized structure reveals a hexagonal P63/mmc (194) symmetry, confirming its stability. As a promising 2D nanomaterial, MXene is widely explored for energy storage applications. Our computed lattice parameters at zero pressure show strong agreement with previous experimental and theoretical findings. The negative cohesive energy further validates the thermodynamic stability and experimental feasibility of Ti3C2 MXene. Electronic structure analysis, including band structure and density of states (DOS), confirms its metallic nature. The optical properties, particularly the reflectivity spectrum, reveal a maximum reflectivity at 0.49 eV, further supporting its metallic behavior. Additionally, mechanical property calculations suggest that Ti3C2 MXene exhibits ductile behavior depending on specific mechanical indicators. These findings provide valuable insights into the potential applications of Ti3C2 in electronic and optoelectronic devices.
articles.summary_en: Density functional theory calculations indicate that Ti3C2 MXene is thermodynamically stable, metallic, optically reflective, and potentially ductile. The findings support further exploration in energy storage, electronic, and optoelectronic devices.

articles.title_original: Defect-engineered Ti3C2Tx MXene/P-doped MoS2 interfaces for Zn2+ storage and electrochemical PFOA detection
articles.title_en: Defect-Engineered MXene/MoS₂ Interfaces Enable Zinc-Ion Storage and PFOA Detection
articles.summary_en: The study develops defect-engineered Ti₃C₂Tₓ MXene/P-doped MoS₂ interfaces for zinc-ion storage and electrochemical detection of PFOA. It links one materials platform to both energy-storage and environmental-sensing applications.

articles.title_original: Versatile Adsorption of Oxygenated Volatile Organic Compounds Using Transition‐Metal‐Decorated Tri‐Unit Anthracene‐Like hBN
articles.title_en: Metal-Decorated hBN Shows Potential for VOC Detection and Capture
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Transition‐metal single‐atom catalysts anchored on two‐dimensional nanostructures provide an effective strategy for tuning electronic properties and gas‐monitoring behavior. In this work, density functional theory calculations are performed to investigate a tri‐unit hexagonal boron nitride framework with an anthracene‐like configuration (Tri‐hBNA) and its single‐atom‐decorated derivatives (Ag, Au, Cu Co, Fe, Ni, Pt, and Zn). Structural and binding‐energy analyses confirm the high thermodynamic stability of pristine and metal‐decorated systems, with metals preferentially anchored at the central region without inducing structural distortion. Metal decoration significantly modulates the wide bandgap of Tri‐hBNA by introducing metal‐derived states and, for magnetic dopants, spin polarization. Gas‐monitoring performance toward methanol and formaldehyde is evaluated via adsorption energies, recovery times, electronic structure, and charge‐transfer analyses. Pristine Tri‐hBNA shows weak physisorption, whereas metal decoration markedly enhances adsorption. Coinage metals favor reversible detection, while Co, Cu, and Ni induce strong chemisorption, indicating potential for gas capture or activation.
articles.summary_en: Density-functional-theory calculations indicate that transition-metal-decorated tri-unit hexagonal boron nitride can substantially enhance adsorption of methanol and formaldehyde. Coinage-metal variants support reversible sensing, while Co-, Cu-, and Ni-decorated systems may enable stronger VOC capture or activation.

articles.title_original: Three-photon photoemission on metallic transition metal dichalcogenide NiTe$_{2}$
articles.title_en: Three-Photon Photoemission Observed in Metallic NiTe₂
articles.excerpt_original: Three-photon photoemission (3PPE) signals on NiTe$_{2}$ are observed for the first time upon ultraviolet excitations. In the energy range beyond two-photon excitations, an energy-momentum dispersive feature is clearly identified with characteristic light polarization dependence. Based on its dispersion, spectral width, as well as intensity as a function of the parallel momentum, this dispersive 3PPE feature could be ascribed to an image potential resonance overlapping with an unoccupied Ni $4s$ -Te $4d$/$5p$ bulk band in accordance with the electronic band structure. Our results underlie higher-order non-linear photoemission on metallic transition metal dichalcogenides and facilitate future ultrafast studies of coherent electron dynamics in anisotropic, two-dimensional systems.
articles.summary_en: Researchers report the first observation of three-photon photoemission from metallic transition-metal dichalcogenide NiTe₂ under ultraviolet excitation. The findings identify an image-potential resonance overlapping with unoccupied bulk bands, supporting future ultrafast studies of electron dynamics in two-dimensional materials.

articles.title_original: Intrinsic Spin Control via Thickness-Vacancy Synergy in 2D Semiconductor for Efficient and Sustainable Photocatalytic Pollutant Removal
articles.title_en: Spin-engineered 2D g-C3N4 boosts photocatalytic pollutant removal
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Intrinsic spin control in two-dimensional (2D) photocatalysts offers a sustainable route for environmental remediation but remains largely unexplored. Herein, a thickness−vacancy synergy strategy was developed to regulate spin density and polarization in g-C3N4 through citric acid-assisted vacancy engineering and thermal exfoliation. The introduction of C vacancies promoted N vacancy formation, while thickness reduction enabled spin polarization at the monolayer limit. The resulting photocatalysts exhibited tunable spin densities that showed a strong positive correlation with pollutant removal performance (R2 = 0.9458). Combined DFT, TRPL, and fs-TA analyses revealed that high spin density suppressed radiative recombination through additional non-radiative pathways, whereas spin polarization enhanced charge separation via spin-selective transfer channels. The optimized catalyst achieved rapid tetracycline degradation (>50% within 5 min) and a 40-fold enhancement in the phenol degradation rate constant. In addition, the system demonstrated low energy consumption, reduced life-cycle impact, and applicability under continuous-flow conditions, complex water matrices, and diverse light sources. This work establishes intrinsic spin engineering as an effective strategy for enhancing photocatalytic pollutant removal and provides a framework for designing high-performance 2D photocatalysts.
articles.summary_en: Researchers used vacancy engineering and thermal exfoliation to control spin density and polarization in 2D graphitic carbon nitride, improving charge separation and suppressing recombination. The optimized catalyst degraded more than 50% of tetracycline within five minutes and increased the phenol degradation rate constant 40-fold, with reported operation under continuous-flow and complex-water conditions.

articles.title_original: Emergence of mixed ionic–van der Waals semiconductors: A first-principles study of 2D InX and TlX monolayers
articles.title_en: First-principles study identifies mixed ionic–van der Waals 2D semiconductors
articles.summary_en: The study investigates InX and TlX monolayers, combining ionic and van der Waals bonding characteristics. Its theoretical findings may inform future exploration of atomically thin semiconductor materials, but no experimental validation or commercial application is indicated.

articles.title_original: Fluorine-Assisted Stabilization of Cubic Phase Boron Nitride Polycrystalline Solids
articles.title_en: Fluorine Stabilizes Cubic Boron Nitride for Hard, Multifunctional Solids
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract The synthesis of cubic boron nitride (cBN) solids by consolidation of cBN powders at high pressure and high temperature (HPHT) is challenging, as it leads to the hexagonal BN (hBN) phase. Here we report an HPHT synthesis of polycrystalline fluorinated cBN (F-cBN) solids that show twinned nanodomains, the presence of F at the grain boundaries, and excellent mechanical hardness and second-order nonlinear susceptibility. In contrast to pure diamagnetic cBN, we found that F-cBN is paramagnetic at room temperature, as confirmed by electron paramagnetic resonance spectroscopy, suggesting the role of defects in tuning the magnetic properties of cBN. Density functional theory calculations reveal that F stabilizes the cBN phase by passivating the dangling bonds and, in addition, forms substitutional defects (FN) leading to FN-VB defect complexes that generate local magnetic moments. These properties of F-cBN might lead to new applications of cBN and also open a pathway to synthesize new metastable phase materials with emergent properties.
articles.summary_en: Researchers synthesized fluorinated cubic boron nitride polycrystalline solids under high pressure and temperature, suppressing conversion to hexagonal BN. The material combines high hardness, nonlinear optical susceptibility, and room-temperature paramagnetism, indicating potential for advanced ceramic and functional-material applications.

articles.title_original: 2D materials with rational design: Advancing electro- and photocatalytic CO2 reduction
articles.title_en: Rationally Designed 2D Materials Advance CO₂ Reduction Catalysis
articles.excerpt_original: CO 2 conversion is central to closing the anthropogenic carbon cycle. However, practical CO 2 RR remains limited by slow molecular activation, competing hydrogen evolution, and dynamic catalyst evolution under operating conditions. Two-dimensional (2D) materials are well suited to address these limitations because their exposed surfaces, short transport pathways, and programmable interfaces allow active sites, charge distribution, local coordination environments, and reaction microenvironments to be tuned with unusual precision. This Review discusses recent advances in 2D-material-based CO 2 RR catalysts across representative families, including graphene, graphitic carbon nitrides (g-C 3 N 4 ), hexagonal boron nitride ( h -BN), 2D transition metal oxides (2D TMOs), 2D transition metal chalcogenides (2D TMDs), layered double hydroxides (LDHs), 2D metal-organic frameworks (2D MOFs), 2D transition metal carbides/nitrides/carbonitrides (MXenes), 2D transition-metal borides (MBenes), phosphorene and borophene. Beyond treating these materials only as separate catalyst classes, the discussion emphasizes cross-cutting design principles from a coordination-chemistry perspective, including defect and doping engineering, surface termination control, interlayer confinement, heterojunction construction, metal-support coordination in isolated single- and dual-atom sites, and composite or tandem architectures. Particular attention is paid to how coordination environments, such as metal-ligand nodes in 2D MOFs, metal‑oxygen motifs in LDHs and TMOs, surface terminations in MXenes, and M–N x sites on 2D supports, regulate CO 2 activation, intermediate binding, charge redistribution, and product selectivity. articles.title_original: Strain Engineering of the Topological Gap and Tunable Chern Numbers in the 2D Kagome Metal-Organic Framework Eu$_2$(C$_6$H$_4$)$_3$
articles.title_en: Strain and Electric Fields Tune Chern States in a 2D Kagome Framework
articles.excerpt_original: The quantum anomalous Hall effect carries dissipationless chiral edge currents without an external magnetic field, yet raising its operating temperature and controlling the number of edge channels remain difficult. Using first-principles calculations, we identify the two-dimensional metal-organic kagome ferromagnet Eu$_2$(C$_6$H$_4$)$_3$ as an intrinsic Chern insulator whose topological gap can be enlarged by mechanical strain. The monolayer has a spin-orbit-coupling-induced gap of 72.7 meV that widens to 124.7 meV under -8% biaxial strain, realizing a quantum anomalous Hall phase with Chern number $\mathcal{C}=-1$ and a single chiral edge state. The local moments come from the half-filled Eu $4f^{7}$ shell, while the gap-opening spin-orbit coupling is carried by Eu $5d$ states hybridized into the carbon kagome bands. The AB-stacked bilayer couples ferromagnetically and accumulates the per-layer Chern numbers, giving $\mathcal{C}=-2$ with two co-propagating chiral channels. An out-of-plane electric field then drives the bilayer through a sequence of topological transitions among $\mathcal{C}=-2$, $-3$, and $-1$, switching the number of edge channels. Together, strain, stacking, and gating give three distinct handles on the gap and the Chern number within a single stoichiometric material.
articles.summary_en: First-principles calculations identify Eu₂(C₆H₄)₃ as an intrinsic Chern insulator whose topological gap increases from 72.7 to 124.7 meV under biaxial strain. articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Developing high-performance noble metal electrocatalysts with accelerated water dissociation and proton transport kinetics under alkaline conditions is critical for scalable green hydrogen production. Herein, we report a Ru@SC‑Ti3C2Tx electrocatalyst constructed via a green and novel supercritical CO2‑mediated solid‑phase etching strategy, which exhibits exceptional HER performance under alkaline conditions. Supercritical CO2, serving as a green solvent, leverages its exceptional penetrability and mass-transfer properties to deliver solid fluoride molecules into the interlayers of MAX phases, enabling selective etching of Al layers under entirely solvent-free conditions. Subsequent loading of ultrafine Ru nanoclusters onto this functionalized MXene support affords the formation of the Ru@SC‑Ti3C2Tx heterostructure electrocatalyst. The optimal catalyst achieves an overpotential of only 14 mV at 10 mA cm−2 in 1 M KOH, with a Tafel slope of 31.5 mV dec−1, and exceptional stability (over 60 h at 100 mA cm−2), outperforming commercial Ru/C (10%) and Pt/C (20%). Operando Raman spectroscopy, electrochemical kinetic analysis, and density functional theory calculations collectively reveal a unique hydrogen spillover mechanism: Ru nanoclusters serve as efficient water dissociation centers, while the SC‑Ti3C2Tx surface acts as an efficient H* acceptor and reservoir, promoting interfacial H* migration. This spatial decoupling of HER elementary steps (H2O activation → H* recombination) synergistically enhances electrochemical reaction kinetics.

articles.title_original: Occurrence of the anomalous quantum Hall effect in monolayer graphene
articles.title_en: Study Reviews Graphene’s Anomalous Quantum Hall Effect
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract This paper provides a pedagogical overview of the anomalous quantum Hall effect in monolayer graphene subjected to a magnetic field perpendicular to the graphene plane. The energy states of the fundamental charge carriers—electrons and holes—are examined using the Dirac–Weyl framework, showing that their Landau level spectrum depends on the square root of the quantum number n , unlike the uniform spacing found in two-dimensional nonrelativistic charge carriers. A distinctive feature of graphene is the zero-energy Landau level, which lies exactly at the Dirac point and is therefore shared equally between the conduction and valence bands. Its spin–valley degeneracy is the same as that of every other level, but only half of its states are counted on the electron side of charge neutrality. This is what produces the characteristic half-integer quantization of the Hall conductivity, the hallmark of the anomalous quantum Hall effect in graphene. The topological origin of this phenomenon is discussed: the pseudospin structure of massless Dirac fermions imparts a Berry phase of π to the Bloch states when encircling a Dirac point, shifting the Landau level index by 1/2 compared to the conventional Schrödinger case. The connection between the degeneracy counting argument and the topological description via the Thouless–Kohmoto–Nightingale–den Nijs formula and the Chern number is made explicit, demonstrating that these two approaches are complementary aspects of the same underlying physics.
articles.summary_en: IOP Publishing presents a pedagogical analysis of the anomalous quantum Hall effect in monolayer graphene. It explains how graphene’s Dirac-like carriers, zero-energy Landau level and Berry phase produce half-integer Hall-conductivity quantization.

articles.title_original: Phason-driven temperature-dependent transport in moiré graphene
articles.title_en: Phasons Drive Temperature-Dependent Transport in Moiré Graphene
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract The electronic and vibrational properties of 2D materials are dramatically altered by the formation of a moiré superlattice. The lowest-energy phonon modes of the superlattice are two acoustic branches (called phasons ) that describe the sliding motion of one layer with respect to the other. Considering their low-energy dispersion and damping, these modes may act as a significant source of scattering for electrons in moiré materials. Here, we investigate temperature-dependent electrical transport in minimally twisted bilayer graphene, a moiré system developing multiple weakly-dispersive electronic bands and a reconstructed lattice structure. We measure a linear-in-temperature resistivity across the band manyfold above T ∼ 10 K, preceded by a quadratic temperature dependence. While the linear-in-temperature resistivity is up to two orders of magnitude larger than in monolayer graphene, it is reduced (approximately by a factor of three) with respect to magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene. Moreover, it is modulated by the recursive band filling, with minima located close to the full filling of each band. Comparing our results with a semiclassical transport calculation, we show that the experimental trends are compatible with scattering processes mediated by longitudinal phasons, which dominate the resistivity over the contribution from conventional acoustic phonons of the monolayer. Our findings highlight the close relation between vibrational modes unique to moiré materials and carrier transport therein.
articles.summary_en: Researchers find that longitudinal phasons—sliding modes between graphene layers—can dominate electrical resistivity in minimally twisted bilayer graphene. The findings clarify how moiré-specific vibrations influence carrier transport and may inform future graphene-based electronic devices.

articles.title_original: Polarizability in Graphene Increases NanoscaleFriction by Amplifying Interfacial EnergyCorrugation
articles.title_en: Graphene Polarizability Increases Nanoscale Water–Graphene Friction
articles.excerpt_original: Early classical molecular dynamics simulations utilizing non-polarizable force fields estimated the water-graphene friction coefficient to be ∼ 1.4×104Nsm−3. However, recent studies have demonstrated that electric polarization and quantum effects beyond the Born-Oppenheimer approximation are crucial for accurately describing nanoscale friction. Observations from recent models suggest that incorporating electric polarization leads to higher predicted friction coefficients. This study evaluates the water-graphene friction coefficient from the SWM4-NDP polarizable water model interacting with both polarizable and non-polarizable graphene models. The friction coefficient is initially computed via equilibrium molecular dynamics (EMD) utilizing the Green-Kubo relation. Given the ongoing debate related to the application of this methodology, the friction coefficient of the fully polarizable system is also evaluated using non-equilibrium molecular dynamics (NEMD). Our EMD calculations show that incorporating explicit electric polarization in graphene increases the interfacial friction coefficient by 23%. Using enhanced-sampling simulations, we obtained that the free-energy landscape of a water monomer is more corrugated on polarizable graphene compared to the non-polarizable model. Quantitative analysis of these landscapes reveals that the friction increase caused by incorporating explicit polarization arises exclusively from a larger lateral force amplitude, which results directly from an enhanced energetic surface corrugation.
articles.summary_en: Molecular-dynamics simulations show that explicitly modeling electric polarization in graphene increases the calculated water–graphene interfacial friction coefficient by 23%. The effect is attributed to greater energetic surface corrugation and lateral force amplitude, refining models of nanoscale interfaces.

articles.title_original: Ultrafast Laser-Induced Photothermoelectric Currents in Graphene Junctions in the Mid-Infrared
articles.title_en: Graphene Junctions Show Ultrafast Mid-Infrared Photothermoelectric Response
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract We investigate the carrier dynamics in graphene junctions under mid-infrared excitation using ultrafast pump–probe photocurrent spectroscopy. We utilize dual split gate devices to demonstrate that the photothermoelectric effect can dominate the photocurrent response of graphene also for a mid-infrared femtosecond excitation. Graphene retains its broadband photocurrent response in this spectral region, but the photocurrent relaxation time increases from ∼2 ps below 8–9 μm up to 3 ps at longer mid-infrared wavelengths. The absence of a pronounced phonon bottleneck in the decay dynamics at room temperature suggests an efficient interplay of electron–electron and electron–phonon scattering even for photon energies below the optical phonon energy in graphene. The observed wavelength dependence of the photocurrent relaxation times is consistent with energy-dependent theoretical relaxation times as derived from a microscopic transport theory of graphene that includes electron–phonon coupling within a Holstein-Peierls Hamiltonian.
articles.summary_en: Researchers found that photothermoelectric effects can dominate photocurrent in graphene junctions under femtosecond mid-infrared excitation. Graphene retains broadband response, while photocurrent relaxation slows from about 2 ps below 8–9 μm to roughly 3 ps at longer wavelengths, supporting potential ultrafast infrared detector development.

articles.title_original: Recent Advances in MXene-Based Cocatalysts for Photocatalytic Hydrogen Evolution
articles.title_en: Review Advances MXene Cocatalysts for Photocatalytic Hydrogen Evolution
articles.excerpt_original: While MXenes are promising cocatalysts for photocatalytic hydrogen evolution, their roles are frequently oversimplified as merely conductive electron sinks. This review begins by revisiting the classical electron-sink mechanism of Ti3C2 and utilizes the CdSe/Ti3C2 and Cd0.5Zn0.5S/Ti3C2 systems to demonstrate how intimate interfaces, Fermi-level equilibration, Schottky junctions, and directional electron-transfer pathways synergistically couple charge separation with H* conversion. The discussion is then extended to multimetallic MXenes, using ZnIn2S4/Mo2TiC2 as a model, to highlight how metal-layer composition, local interfacial coordination, work-function differences, and hydrogen-adsorption energetics jointly regulate electron extraction and surface reaction kinetics. Special attention is given to surface terminations, which can reshape interfacial energetics and enable MXenes to transition between electron-sink and hole-mediated roles depending on the interface and working conditions. Furthermore, representative Nb2C quantum-dot and VNbC solid-solution systems illustrate how nanoscale electric fields and multimetallic sites can expand MXene functionality beyond conventional electron extraction. Ultimately, this role-oriented framework advances the development of MXene cocatalysts from simple material integration toward controllable and programmable interfacial functions.
articles.summary_en: A review reframes MXenes as multifunctional cocatalysts whose interfacial structures, work functions, surface terminations and multimetallic compositions govern charge separation and hydrogen-production kinetics. It highlights pathways beyond conventional electron-sink behavior, including hole-mediated roles, nanoscale electric fields and multimetallic active sites.
